title: What Great Agents Should Expect From Their Loan Officer
description: The right lending partner helps agents win offers and close on time. Here's what a strong agent and loan officer relationship looks like and how to set it up.
image_alt: A woman in a suit showing a document to a man

faq.q: How quickly should a loan officer respond to an agent?
faq.a: On active deals, same day is the standard to expect, especially when an offer is being written or a deadline is approaching.

faq.q: Should a loan officer call the listing agent?
faq.a: Yes. A quick call to the listing agent to vouch for the buyer's approval can strengthen an offer, especially in multiple-offer situations.

faq.q: What should agents send the loan officer after acceptance?
faq.a: The fully executed contract, all addenda, escrow and title contacts, and the contingency removal dates.

body_html:
Agents spend a lot of energy finding the right home for a client. The loan officer on the other side of that offer can make it stronger or weaker without anyone noticing until it's too late. After years of leading loan teams, here's what I believe agents should expect from a lending partner, and what makes the relationship work both ways.

Before the offer

  • A real pre-approval. Credit pulled, income and assets reviewed, and any issues flagged up front. See my post on pre-qualification vs. pre-approval for the distinction.
  • Fast letter updates. A letter matched to each offer price, turned around quickly, including evenings and weekends when it matters.
  • Straight answers about risk. If the property type, price, or buyer profile creates a challenge, you should hear about it before you write, not after.

During the offer

When an offer goes in, I believe the loan officer should be willing to call the listing agent directly. A two-minute conversation that says "I've reviewed this buyer's file, here's where we stand, and here's my cell" can move an offer up the pile. Listing agents are evaluating closing risk as much as price.

During escrow

What to expectWhy it matters
Appraisal ordered immediatelyThe appraisal is often the longest lead-time item
Proactive weekly updatesNo one should have to chase status
Early warning on problemsTime to solve issues before deadlines
Clear sign-off before contingency removalProtects your client's deposit
Closing Disclosure on scheduleAvoids last-minute timing problems

What makes it a two-way relationship

Loan officers do their best work when agents help with a few things too:

  1. Send the executed contract and all addenda the moment they're signed
  2. Share contingency dates and any special terms right away
  3. Loop the loan officer in before agreeing to credits or price changes, so we can confirm the loan supports them; see seller credits and concessions
  4. Encourage buyers to send documents quickly

Why the broker channel helps agents

As a mortgage broker, my team can compare options across multiple wholesale lenders. For agents, that means fewer dead ends. If one lender's guidelines don't fit a self-employed buyer, a condo, or a jumbo loan, there's often another that does. It also means more ways to compete on pricing and turn times for your clients.

Red flags in a lending partner

Just as there are signs of a great loan officer, there are warning signs worth noticing early:

  • Pre-approval letters issued without documents or credit review
  • Voicemail-only communication during offer weekends
  • Surprises at contingency removal that should have been caught weeks earlier
  • Vague answers when asked about a buyer's file status
  • Last-minute changes to cash to close or loan terms without explanation

Any one of these can happen occasionally. A pattern is a reason to rethink who you send your clients to, because your reputation is tied to how their financing goes.

Setting expectations in the first conversation

The best partnerships start with a frank conversation about how each side likes to work. How do you prefer updates: text, email, or calls? Who should the loan officer contact if the buyer is unresponsive? How do you want to handle listing agent calls? A few minutes on these questions up front avoids friction on every deal afterward.

From my side, I also want to know what kinds of buyers and properties you work with most. That lets my team prepare for the scenarios you're most likely to bring, from jumbo loans to first-time buyer programs.

The takeaway

A great loan officer makes your offers stronger, your escrows calmer, and your clients happier. Expect real pre-approvals, fast communication, and honest risk assessments, and give your lending partner the information they need to deliver. If you're an agent looking for that kind of partner in Southern California, I'd welcome a conversation.
